html:
The doctrine of lapse was the rule by which the East India Company took over Indian states whose ruler died without a son of his own. Lord Dalhousie, governor-general from 1848 to 1856, used it to annex seven states in eight years.

Hindu law and custom let a king without a son adopt an heir. Dalhousie held that in states dependent on the Company an adopted son could inherit the king's private property but not the throne, unless the British had agreed in advance. Without that, the state "lapsed" to the Company.

Satara went in 1848, then Sambalpur, Nagpur and others. Jhansi was taken in 1854; its queen, Lakshmibai, was told her adopted son would not rule. The adopted heir of the last Maratha peshwa was refused his pension. In 1856 Dalhousie also annexed Awadh, a large kingdom, on the ground of misrule.

He believed direct British rule was better for the people and more profitable. He also built railways, telegraphs and a postal service (see the first train).

The annexations frightened every prince and put thousands of soldiers and courtiers out of work. They were a main cause of the Indian Rebellion of 1857. In 1858 the Crown promised to take no more territory and to accept adoptions.
